questions.prompt: Which conjugate base is most stabilized by resonance?
options: CH₃O⁻
CH₃CO₂⁻
CH₃CH₂⁻
NH₂⁻

feedback.hint: Look for equivalent or near-equivalent atoms that can share charge through π bonding.
feedback.solution: The acetate ion delocalizes negative charge over two oxygen atoms. The other listed anions lack comparable resonance stabilization.

questions.prompt: A tertiary alkyl halide in water undergoes substitution. Which pathway is generally more plausible?
options: SN2, because the tertiary center is unhindered
SN1, because ionization can form a stabilized carbocation
Neither pathway can occur in a protic solvent
A radical chain is required

feedback.hint: Tertiary substitution centers are strongly sterically hindered for backside attack.
feedback.solution: SN1 is generally favored for a tertiary center in a polar protic solvent because carbocation formation is stabilized and SN2 is sterically hindered. The actual pathway depends on the full substrate and conditions.

questions.prompt: Which geometric arrangement is required for a typical concerted E2 elimination?
options: Anti-periplanar C–H and C–leaving-group bonds
Any arrangement because the carbocation rotates
A tetrahedral carbon with no beta hydrogen
An aromatic ring with all sigma bonds fixed

feedback.hint: E2 forms the π bond as the C–H and C–leaving-group bonds break together.
feedback.solution: The required orbital alignment is usually anti-periplanar; in a cyclohexane chair this is trans-diaxial.

modifications: Clarified the typical E2 answer option as anti-periplanar; atypical syn elimination is not presented as equally typical.

questions.prompt: Why are acid chlorides generally more reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution than amides?
options: Chloride is a better leaving group and donates less by resonance
Amide carbonyl carbon is more electrophilic
Amides have no carbonyl resonance
Chloride prevents nucleophilic attack

feedback.hint: Compare leaving-group basicity and resonance donation into the carbonyl.
feedback.solution: Chloride is a weaker base and better leaving group than an amide anion, while nitrogen donates strongly by resonance and reduces amide carbonyl electrophilicity.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the carboxylate ion's resonance structures is correct?
options: Only electrons move between the structures; the real ion is a hybrid with two equivalent C–O bonds of intermediate length.
The ion flips rapidly between two different molecules.
Each structure is an isolated species present in solution.
Atoms move to new positions between structures.

feedback.hint: Recall what resonance does and does not describe.
feedback.solution: Resonance structures differ only in electron placement with the same atom positions and valences. The actual ion is a single delocalized hybrid, so both C–O bonds are equivalent with bond order about 1.5.

questions.prompt: A chiral secondary alkyl bromide reacts with cyanide by a concerted backside attack. What are the stereochemical and rate consequences?
options: Retention of configuration with a rate that depends on substrate only.
Loss of stereochemistry and a zero-order rate.
Racemization with a first-order rate in substrate.
Inversion of configuration at carbon, with a rate that depends on both the substrate and the nucleophile concentration.

feedback.hint: Backside attack in one step gives a specific geometric outcome and a bimolecular rate.
feedback.solution: A concerted SN2 step inverts the carbon center, and because both reactants are in the one rate-determining step the rate is second order overall: rate = k[RBr][CN⁻].

questions.prompt: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of 2-methyl-2-butanol through a carbocation intermediate gives mainly which alkene, assuming Zaitsev selectivity?
options: 2-methyl-1-butene as the major product.
2-methyl-2-butene, the more substituted alkene.
No alkene forms.
3-methyl-1-butene as the major product.

feedback.hint: The more substituted alkene is usually more stable.
feedback.solution: Loss of a proton from the carbon that leads to the more substituted double bond gives 2-methyl-2-butene as the major product under thermodynamic (Zaitsev) control. The assumption can fail with bulky bases or when other pathways compete.

questions.prompt: Which pairing correctly states the reaction type?
options: A Grignard reagent with a ketone undergoes nucleophilic addition; an amine with an acid chloride undergoes nucleophilic acyl substitution.
Both are electrophilic aromatic substitutions.
A Grignard reagent with a ketone is an acyl substitution; an amine with an acid chloride is an addition.
Both are eliminations.

feedback.hint: Look for a leaving group on the carbonyl carbon.
feedback.solution: Ketones lack a good leaving group, so a nucleophile adds to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated. Acid chlorides have a good leaving group (chloride), so the addition intermediate collapses and expels it, giving net substitution.

questions.prompt: Which ordering of reactivity toward nucleophilic acyl substitution is correct?
options: Amide > ester > thioester, because nitrogen is the most electronegative.
Thioester > ester > amide, because sulfur donates less resonance stabilization to the carbonyl than oxygen, and nitrogen donates the most.
All three react at the same rate.
Ester > thioester > amide, because oxygen is a better leaving group than sulfur.

feedback.hint: Consider resonance donation into the carbonyl and leaving-group basicity.
feedback.solution: Nitrogen's strong resonance donation stabilizes amides; sulfur's poor 3p–2p overlap gives thioesters little stabilization and a weaker-base leaving group. Hence acetyl-CoA is an activated acyl donor while peptide bonds persist.

questions.prompt: A histidine side chain has pKa 6.0. What percentage is protonated at pH 7.4? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Protonated fraction of a base = 1/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)).

questions.prompt: A lysine side-chain amine has pKa 10.5. What percentage is unprotonated (nucleophilic) at pH 7.4? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Unprotonated fraction = 1 − protonated fraction = 1/(1 + 10^(pKa − pH)).

questions.prompt: A site is modified with first-order rate constant 0.01 per year; the protein is replaced with a half-life of 10 years. Using f_ss = k_m/(k_m + k_d), calculate the steady-state modified fraction. Enter a decimal fraction, number only.

feedback.hint: Convert the half-life to k_d = ln 2 / t½ first.

questions.prompt: With the same modification rate (0.01 per year), a protein is replaced with a half-life of 2 days. Calculate the steady-state modified fraction. Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Convert days to years before computing k_d.

questions.prompt: Glucose is mostly a cyclic hemiacetal in water, yet it slowly modifies lysine residues. What is the first chemical step?
options: The cyclic form transfers a phosphate to lysine.
The small open-chain fraction's aldehyde is attacked by an unprotonated amine, forming an imine (Schiff base) after loss of water.
Glucose forms an amide bond with lysine directly.
Protonated lysine attacks the ring oxygen.

feedback.hint: Which functional group of glucose is electrophilic, and which form of lysine is nucleophilic?
feedback.solution: Carbonyl addition by a neutral amine followed by dehydration gives an imine, which can rearrange to the Amadori ketoamine. Both partners must be in their minor reactive forms, which is one reason the reaction is slow.

questions.prompt: tert-Butyl bromide is dissolved in water with no added strong nucleophile. Which mechanism and rate law best describe substitution?
options: SN2, because water is a strong nucleophile.
No substitution can occur at a tertiary carbon.
SN1; rate = k[substrate], because the tertiary carbocation is stabilized and the protic solvent stabilizes ions.
SN2; rate = k[substrate][water].

feedback.hint: Consider steric access for back-side attack and carbocation stability.
feedback.solution: Tertiary carbons block back-side attack but form stable carbocations. A polar protic solvent and weak nucleophile favor SN1, whose rate does not depend on the nucleophile.

questions.prompt: An SN2 reaction has k = 2×10⁻³ L mol⁻¹ s⁻¹. What is the rate when [substrate] = 0.1 M and [nucleophile] = 0.4 M? Enter the number only (mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹).

feedback.hint: Rate = k[substrate][nucleophile].
feedback.solution: 2×10⁻³ × 0.1 × 0.4 = 8.0×10⁻⁵ mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹, twice the rate at 0.2 M.

questions.prompt: An enantiomerically pure secondary alkyl bromide undergoes clean SN2 substitution. What happens at the stereocenter?
options: Its configuration is retained.
It racemizes.
The stereocenter is destroyed permanently.
Its configuration is inverted, because the nucleophile attacks from the side opposite the leaving group.

feedback.hint: Picture the back-side attack.
feedback.solution: SN2 proceeds through a single back-side attack, inverting the geometry (Walden inversion). Racemization is characteristic of SN1 through a planar carbocation.

questions.prompt: A molecule has 3 stereocenters and no internal symmetry. What is the maximum number of stereoisomers? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Each stereocenter can be R or S.

questions.prompt: A pure enantiomer has specific rotation -11.5°; a sample shows -9.2° under the same conditions. What is the enantiomeric excess? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: ee = observed/pure × 100.

questions.prompt: A sample has 80% enantiomeric excess. What percentage of it is the major enantiomer? Enter a value and unit.

feedback.hint: Major = (100 + ee)/2.
